subject: ELA
overview: Each week combines a reading text, word study or grammar mini-lesson, a writing product and discussion. Read each text yourself first, read aloud together when the text is hard, and always ask your child to point to the exact words that support an answer. Writing moves through planning, drafting, revising and publishing — keep a portfolio. Fridays check progress; use the rubrics to give specific feedback.

weeks.prep: Find 'Eleven' by Sandra Cisneros (from Woman Hollering Creek, or an anthology) and read it yourself first; it is short (about 3 pages). Gather a composition notebook and highlighters. Have a timer ready for the 1-minute fluency read.
misconceptions: Treating a quotation as evidence without explaining it. Teach 'quote, then explain': follow every quotation with 'This shows…'.
Copying words without quotation marks or changing the wording. Evidence in quotation marks must match the text exactly.
Confusing 'because' (conjunction joining a reason) with a sentence fragment ('Because she was sad.'). A 'because' clause needs a main clause attached.

days.guide: Read 'Eleven' aloud, then reread the opening while your child highlights each comparison Rachel makes about growing older (an onion, the rings inside a tree trunk, little wooden dolls that fit one inside the other). Ask what the comparisons have in common and what they show about how she feels on her birthday.

questions.q: What does Rachel compare growing older to, and what does that show?
questions.a: An onion, the rings inside a tree trunk, and nesting wooden dolls — each year sits inside the next. It shows she feels that all her younger ages (like three and ten) are still inside her, which is why she can feel little and cry even though she is eleven.

days.guide: Model one inference question with an exact quotation ('Mrs. Price says…') and explain it. Your child answers 4 inference questions, copying sentences word for word inside quotation marks. Mini-lesson: and joins, but contrasts, because gives a reason; have them write one sentence with each.

questions.q: How does Mrs. Price treat Rachel? Quote the text.
questions.a: She does not believe Rachel: she insists the ugly red sweater is Rachel's because Sylvia Saldívar said so, puts it on Rachel's desk and makes her put it on. Strong answers quote her words that she remembers Rachel wearing it, or her order to put it on.

questions.q: Join with a conjunction: Rachel cried. The sweater wasn't hers.
questions.a: Rachel cried because the sweater wasn't hers.

days.guide: Show your own notebook page: a heart drawn and filled with people, places and things you care about. Your child makes a heart map and a timeline of 10 small moments (a few minutes long each, not whole vacations) to use for narratives.

questions.q: Which is a 'small moment': 'my summer vacation' or 'the second my dog ran into the lake'?
questions.a: The second one — a narrative works best focused on a short, specific event.

days.guide: Discuss 'Is Rachel's reaction fair?' using stems such as 'I agree/disagree because on page __ it says…'. Then have your child read a passage aloud for exactly 1 minute; count words read correctly and record the WPM as a baseline.

questions.q: Why doesn't Rachel just tell Mrs. Price clearly that it isn't hers?
questions.a: She is a child and Mrs. Price is the adult in charge; she feels small and her younger ages take over, so she can only get out a few words before she starts to cry.

days.guide: Your child writes a paragraph explaining how first-person point of view (Rachel telling her own story) affects the story, with two quotations. Then give a 10-sentence conjunction quiz (circle the conjunction, label its job).

questions.q: How does first person affect the story?
questions.a: We hear Rachel's private thoughts — what she wishes she had said and her wish to be 102 — so we feel her embarrassment directly; we only see Mrs. Price through Rachel's eyes.

weeks.assessment_key: Evidence paragraph rubric: 4 = clear claim about point of view, two exact quotations with correct quotation marks, each explained; 3 = claim and two quotations with partial explanation; 2 = one quotation or paraphrase only; 1 = no evidence. Conjunction quiz: student circles and labels and (adds), but (contrasts), because (reason), or (choice), so (result) correctly in 8 of 10 sentences for proficiency. Fluency: record WPM (typical fall grade 5 is roughly 110–125 WPM).

weeks.prep: Download 'The Ransom of Red Chief' (O. Henry, in Whirligigs on Project Gutenberg) and preview it. Parental note: the story uses dated 1900s vocabulary and includes the boy playing 'Indian' with stereotyped language; plan to discuss why that is hurtful today. Prepare a story map and Venn diagram.
misconceptions: Thinking irony is just coincidence. Situational irony is when the outcome is the opposite of what is expected (kidnappers pay the father).
Writing a summary that retells every detail. A summary hits beginning, conflict, turning point and ending in about 5 sentences.
Confusing prepositions with adverbs. A preposition always has an object: 'up the tree' (prepositional phrase) vs. 'climbed up' (adverb).

days.guide: Partner-read the story, stopping to explain old words (ransom, diatribe, palatable). Your child marks each moment the plan backfires with a sticky note. Discuss the stereotyped 'Indian' play and why it is offensive.

questions.q: What is Sam and Bill's plan, and how does it backfire?
questions.a: They kidnap Ebenezer Dorset's son to collect a ransom, but the boy ('Red Chief') loves camping out and torments Bill so badly that the kidnappers end up desperate to get rid of him.

days.guide: Teach the five prefixes (un- = not, re- = again, dis- = not/opposite, mis- = wrongly, pre- = before). Your child sorts and defines 20 words, then reads 10 long story words by syllables.

questions.q: What does 'misjudge' mean? 'preheat'?
questions.a: To judge wrongly; to heat before.

questions.q: Divide and read 'philanthropist'.
questions.a: phil-an-thro-pist.

days.guide: Fill the Venn diagram with three details for Bill and Sam and three for Red Chief (e.g., Red Chief: wild, energetic, enjoys himself). Your child writes a 5-sentence plot summary.

questions.q: How does the ransom end?
questions.a: Dorset refuses to pay and instead offers to take his son back if the kidnappers pay him $250; Sam and Bill pay and hurry away.

questions.q: What do Bill and Sam have in common?
questions.a: Both are small-time crooks who want money and both end up exhausted and outsmarted by the boy.

days.guide: Your child picks a small moment and fills the story arc. Mini-lesson: underline prepositional phrases (in the cave, after dinner); write 5 sentences with them.

questions.q: Underline the prepositional phrase: Red Chief hid behind the rock.
questions.a: behind the rock (preposition: behind; object: rock).

days.guide: Give a short reading check (situational irony, sequence of 5 events) and a 10-word prefix quiz, then your child tells the story arc aloud. Check that your child explains the irony in their own words (kidnappers end up paying) and gets the 5 events in order.

questions.q: Why is the ending situational irony?
questions.a: We expect the father to pay the kidnappers, but the kidnappers pay the father.

weeks.assessment_key: Summary/Venn: 4 = 5-sentence summary with conflict, turning point and the twist ending (kidnappers pay $250), three accurate details per character; 3 = accurate but missing one element; 2 = retelling with errors; 1 = incomplete. Prefix quiz key (sample): unhappy = not happy; reread = read again; disagree = not agree; misspell = spell wrongly; preview = view before; unlock, redo, dishonest, misplace, prepay similarly. Narrative plan: beginning, rising action, climax, resolution all filled for one small moment.

weeks.prep: Print 'Thank You, Ma'am' (CommonLit) and read it first — about 4 pages. Make a dialogue punctuation anchor chart: “Hello,” she said. / She said, “Hello.” / “Why,” he asked, “are you here?”
misconceptions: Putting the comma outside the closing quotation mark. In American English commas and periods go inside.
Starting a new paragraph only for each new sentence. Start a new paragraph each time the speaker changes.
Writing a theme as one word ('kindness'). A theme is a full statement: 'Kindness can change a person more than punishment.'

days.guide: Read the story aloud. Your child records what Mrs. Jones does at three points (when Roger grabs her purse; at her home; at the end) and writes a theme statement supported by those actions.

questions.q: What does Mrs. Jones do instead of calling the police?
questions.a: She drags Roger to her home, has him wash his face, feeds him, and gives him ten dollars for the blue suede shoes he wanted.

questions.q: Write a theme statement.
questions.a: Example: Treating someone with trust and kindness can teach more than punishment can.

days.guide: Read aloud a stretch of dialogue and ask what it shows about each character. Your child punctuates 10 dialogue lines and adds interjections (Oh! Well,).

questions.q: Punctuate: you could have asked me she said
questions.a: “You could have asked me,” she said.

questions.q: Add an interjection: That hurts!
questions.a: “Ouch! That hurts!” (or Oh, that hurts!)

days.guide: Your child drafts three different openings for the personal narrative: action, dialogue, sensory detail. Read them aloud and choose the strongest.

questions.q: Which lead type is this: “Don't let go!” Dad yelled.
questions.a: Dialogue lead.

days.guide: Your child drafts the rest of the narrative including at least 4 lines of correctly punctuated dialogue and a series of sensory details with commas. Read the draft back together and put a check beside each dialogue line that shows a new speaker on a new line.

questions.q: Punctuate the series: The kitchen smelled of cinnamon apples and burnt toast.
questions.a: The kitchen smelled of cinnamon, apples, and burnt toast. (Serial comma optional but consistent.)

days.guide: Discuss theme with stems ('I think… because in the text…'), then give a 10-item dialogue and series-comma quiz. Listen for a 'because' tied to a specific action of Mrs. Jones, then grade the quiz with the anchor chart beside you.

questions.q: Why does Roger say only 'Thank you, ma'am' at the end?
questions.a: He is so moved by her kindness that he can't find words for what he wants to say; the text says he wanted to say more but couldn't.

weeks.assessment_key: Theme statement: proficient = complete-sentence theme (e.g., kindness and trust can change a person) supported by two of Mrs. Jones's actions. Narrative draft: complete beginning/middle/end, 4+ dialogue lines. Punctuation quiz key: commas/periods inside quotation marks; capital letter starting each quote; new paragraph per speaker; commas between 3+ items in a series; interjection followed by ! or ,.

weeks.prep: Find 'All Summer in a Day' by Ray Bradbury (library anthology or CommonLit) and read it first. Note: the children lock Margot in a closet — a bullying scene worth discussing. Prepare a revision checklist and colored pens. Choose an unfamiliar short story for the Friday cold read.
misconceptions: Thinking setting is just the place. Setting includes time and conditions; here the constant rain on Venus causes the conflict.
Revising means just fixing spelling. Revising changes content (adding detail, slowing a moment); editing fixes conventions.
Shifting verb tense in the middle of a narrative. Pick past tense and keep it.

days.guide: Read the story and list words describing rain and sun. Discuss how the setting — Venus, where it has rained for seven years and the sun appears for only about two hours every seven years — causes the conflict with Margot.

questions.q: Why are the children jealous of Margot?
questions.a: She came from Earth (Ohio) only five years ago and remembers the sun; they were too young to remember it.

questions.q: How does the setting cause the conflict?
questions.a: The endless rain makes the sun precious; Margot's memory of it sets her apart, and the children lock her in a closet just before the sun comes out.

days.guide: Your child finds the most important moment in the narrative and stretches it into at least a full paragraph with thoughts, feelings and sensory details. Model first with a dull sentence ('I was scared') stretched into several sentences of heartbeat, thoughts and sounds. Then have your child highlight the stretched moment in the draft.

questions.q: Name three things you can add to slow down a moment.
questions.a: Thoughts, feelings, sensory details (sounds, smells), small actions, dialogue.

days.guide: Edit with the checklist (dialogue punctuation, series commas, spelling, consistent tense), then your child reads aloud to catch errors. Have your child mark each fix in colored pen so you can see what they caught; catch only patterns they missed, not every error.

questions.q: Fix the tense: I ran to the door and I see my dad.
questions.a: I ran to the door and I saw my dad.

days.guide: Your child types the final narrative and reads it aloud in an 'author's chair' to family who respond with one compliment and one question. Aim for one sitting; afterward ask, 'Which part are you proudest of and why?'

questions.q: What makes a strong ending to a personal narrative?
questions.a: It resolves the moment and shows what the narrator felt, learned, or realized.

days.guide: Give the cold-read assessment on an unfamiliar story (theme, character, quoting evidence) and a vocabulary quiz on prefixes and roots from weeks 1–3. Do not help during the cold read; afterward score with the rubric and review one question together.

questions.q: At the end of 'All Summer in a Day,' how do the children feel when they let Margot out?
questions.a: Ashamed and guilty — they can't look at each other and move slowly to unlock the door.

weeks.assessment_key: Narrative rubric (4 levels): 4 = focused small moment, engaging lead, the key moment slowed with thoughts/sensory detail, correctly punctuated dialogue, satisfying ending, few errors; 3 = all parts present with minor gaps; 2 = summary-like, little detail or many errors; 1 = incomplete. Cold-read rubric (choose an unfamiliar grade-5 story from CommonLit): 4 = states a precise theme/central idea, explains character with 2+ exact quotations correctly punctuated and explained; 3 = accurate answer with at least one relevant quotation and explanation; 2 = accurate but general answer, evidence paraphrased or loosely connected; 1 = inaccurate or no evidence. Vocabulary quiz: prefixes un-/re-/dis-/mis-/pre- defined correctly.

weeks.prep: Borrow Hatchet by Gary Paulsen and preview chapters 1–4. Parental note: chapter 1–2 describe the pilot's fatal heart attack; 'the Secret' is that Brian saw his mother kissing a man who was not his father — be ready to discuss divorce. Find a map of northern Canada.
misconceptions: Mixing up internal and external conflict. External = against nature or others (crash, hunger); internal = inside the mind (fear, the Secret).
Thinking a flashback is a dream. A flashback interrupts the present to show an earlier event.
Using 'had' for every past action. Past perfect (had flown) shows an action finished before another past action.

days.guide: Read chapters 1–2. Your child copies 3 sentences or fragments that build suspense (short, repeated phrases) and explains how one makes the reader feel.

questions.q: What happens to the pilot, and why is Brian in danger?
questions.a: The pilot has a heart attack and dies; Brian, who has never flown a plane, is alone in a small bush plane over the Canadian wilderness.

questions.q: Why does Paulsen use short fragments during the emergency?
questions.a: They imitate Brian's panicked thoughts and speed up the pace, building suspense.

days.guide: Read chapter 3; identify the flashback to 'the Secret' and discuss how memories interrupt the present in the opening chapters. Ask your child to find the exact words where the present story shifts into memory and back.

questions.q: What is 'the Secret'?
questions.a: Brian saw his mother in a car kissing a man who wasn't his father; his parents are divorced and he hasn't told his father.

questions.q: Why include the flashback?
questions.a: It reveals Brian's internal conflict and the emotional pain he carries into the survival story.

days.guide: Teach perfect tenses: present perfect (has crashed), past perfect (had crashed), future perfect (will have crashed). Your child writes 9 sentences about the crash, 3 per tense.

questions.q: Write in past perfect: Brian (land) the plane before he realized he was hurt.
questions.a: Brian had landed the plane before he realized he was hurt.

questions.q: Name the tense: By tomorrow, Brian will have spent three days alone.
questions.a: Future perfect.

days.guide: Read chapter 4 and fill a two-column chart of internal and external conflicts with page numbers. Model one row of the chart first, then let your child complete at least 3 of each type.

questions.q: Give one internal and one external conflict.
questions.a: Internal: fear, self-pity, memories of the Secret. External: hunger, thirst, mosquitoes, being lost in the wilderness.

days.guide: Discuss 'What would you do first?' using evidence, then give a chapters 1–4 quiz with perfect-tense items. During discussion, require each idea to be tied to something Brian actually had or knew in the book.

questions.q: What gift did Brian's mother give him?
questions.a: A hatchet, which he wears on his belt.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key (suggested): 1) Brian is 13 and flying to visit his father in the Canadian oil fields 2) the pilot has a heart attack 3) Brian crash-lands the plane into a lake 4) his mother gave him the hatchet 5) the Secret = he saw his mother with another man 6) internal conflict example: fear/memories 7) external example: hunger/insects 8) 'had landed' = past perfect 9) 'has survived' = present perfect 10) 'will have waited' = future perfect. Journal entries: complete, dated, with at least one quotation.

weeks.prep: Preview Hatchet chapters 5–9 and a ReadWorks article on wilderness survival. Sticky notes for marking decisions.
misconceptions: Calling every comparison a simile. Simile uses like/as; metaphor says something is something else; personification gives human traits.
Main idea = topic. The main idea is what the author says about the topic.
Explaining figurative language literally. Ask 'what does this show about Brian's situation or feelings?'

days.guide: Read chapters 5–6; your child marks three decisions Brian makes (drinking lake water, eating berries, choosing a shelter) and rates each smart or risky with evidence. Model one rating with a page number, then your child does the other two. Ask, 'What would a safer choice have been?'

questions.q: Was it smart for Brian to drink so much lake water?
questions.a: Risky — he drank too much at first and got sick; drinking slowly was safer.

days.guide: Your child collects 6 examples of figurative language from chapters 5–7 and explains what each shows. Check each label (simile/metaphor/personification).

questions.q: Label: The wind whispered through the trees.
questions.a: Personification — wind cannot whisper; it suggests a quiet, eerie setting.

days.guide: Read the survival article; identify two main ideas and compare its advice (shelter, water, fire, signaling) with Brian's choices. Have your child underline each piece of advice in the article and put a check if Brian followed it.

questions.q: How does Brian's choice of shelter compare with survival advice?
questions.a: Survival guides stress finding shelter early; Brian builds a lean-to under a rock overhang near the lake, which follows that advice.

days.guide: Read chapters 8–9 (porcupine and fire). Your child writes a journal entry explaining why the hatchet becomes so important.

questions.q: How does Brian discover how to make fire?
questions.a: He throws the hatchet at a porcupine in the dark, it hits the rock wall and makes sparks; he then strikes the hatchet on the rock to light birch bark.

questions.q: Why does the hatchet become so important?
questions.a: It is his only tool: it makes fire and lets him build and hunt.

days.guide: Give a chapters 5–9 quiz with figurative language items. Then practice verb tense for sequence in 5 sentences (e.g., After he had found the berries, he ate them).

questions.q: Combine with tense showing sequence: He found the berries. He got sick.
questions.a: After he had eaten the berries, he got sick.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key (suggested): 1) Brian builds his shelter under a rock overhang 2) the 'gut cherries' make him sick 3) he finds raspberries later 4) a porcupine quills his leg 5) sparks from the hatchet on rock make fire 6) simile, metaphor, personification correctly labeled in 3 examples. Figurative language chart: 6 examples, correct labels, explanation of meaning. Journal entry: claim about the hatchet with at least one quotation.

weeks.prep: Preview chapters 10–13 of Hatchet. Parental note: at Brian's low point after the search plane passes without seeing him, he tries to harm himself with the hatchet (described briefly). Read this section first and be ready to talk about it calmly and to emphasize that he chooses to live and that people should always reach out for help.
misconceptions: Thinking character change happens all at once. Show it builds over many small experiences.
Shifting tense mid-paragraph. Pick past tense for the scene and keep it.
Confusing roots with prefixes: 'port' is a root meaning carry; 'trans-' is a prefix.

days.guide: Read chapters 10–11. Your child builds a T-chart: 'old Brian' (city boy, self-pity) vs. 'new Brian' (observant, patient) with quotations.

questions.q: Give one example of the 'new Brian.'
questions.a: He learns to watch and listen closely, gathers turtle eggs, and makes a fish spear — he solves problems instead of feeling sorry for himself.

days.guide: Teach spect (see), port (carry), struct (build), rupt (break). Your child builds 16 words and defines any found in Hatchet.

questions.q: What do 'inspect,' 'transport,' 'construct' and 'erupt' mean?
questions.a: Look at closely; carry across; build; break out.

days.guide: Read chapters 12–13. Discuss the turning point: the search plane passes without seeing him, his despair, and his decision to keep going as a tougher 'new' person.

questions.q: How does the passing plane change Brian?
questions.a: He loses hope and hits his lowest point, but afterward he becomes determined and tough, realizing self-pity doesn't help.

days.guide: Your child writes a one-page scene from an animal's view watching Brian, staying in one tense. Before writing, list what the animal could see, hear and smell. After writing, your child circles every verb to check the tense stays the same.

questions.q: Which tense works best for a story scene?
questions.a: Usually past tense, kept consistent from beginning to end.

days.guide: Your child corrects 10 sentences with tense shifts and takes a roots quiz. For each fix, have your child say which word signaled the time (yesterday, then) and which tense it requires.

questions.q: Fix: Brian sharpens the spear and then he threw it.
questions.a: Brian sharpened the spear and then he threw it.

weeks.assessment_key: Roots quiz key: spect = see (spectator, inspect); port = carry (portable, import); struct = build (structure, instruct); rupt = break (rupture, interrupt). T-chart: 3+ contrasting traits with quotations. Animal scene rubric: consistent point of view and tense, sensory detail, accurate to events in Hatchet.

weeks.prep: Preview Hatchet chapters 14–17 (the moose attack and the tornado). Draw a plot mountain. Set up a phone to record the fluency reading.
misconceptions: Thinking theme equals a story event. Theme is the lesson about life (e.g., resilience), not what happened.
Choosing evidence that only retells. Pick quotations that show Brian's attitude.
Reading dramatic passages too fast. Model pausing at commas and slowing for important moments.

days.guide: Read chapters 14–15. Your child plots major events so far on a plot mountain (crash, fire, low point, new Brian…).

questions.q: What is the climax-building pattern of the novel?
questions.a: Each problem (hunger, fire, shelter) is followed by a small victory, building toward greater challenges.

days.guide: Read chapter 16. Your child lists what Brian lost and what he still has after the moose attack and the tornado, and explains his reaction.

questions.q: How does Brian react to losing his shelter and supplies?
questions.a: He is hurt and discouraged but does not give up; he starts rebuilding, showing he has changed.

days.guide: Read chapter 17; hold a conversation on resilience. Your child cites two page numbers.

questions.q: What does Brian notice after the tornado that gives him new hope?
questions.a: The tail of the plane is now sticking up out of the lake, and he remembers there may be a survival pack inside.

days.guide: Your child reads a dramatic passage from chapter 16 three times with expression, then records the best reading. Model one reading with expression yourself first. Compare the first and final recordings together and name one improvement.

questions.q: What makes reading 'with expression'?
questions.a: Changing pace, volume and tone to match the action and feelings; pausing at punctuation.

days.guide: Your child writes a theme paragraph on 'What does Hatchet teach about mistakes?' with two quotations. Remind your child to use the quote sandwich (introduce, quote, explain). Score with the rubric and point to one strong sentence.

questions.q: State a theme about mistakes.
questions.a: Mistakes are how we learn: Brian fails often (sick from berries, porcupine quills) but each mistake teaches him to survive.

weeks.assessment_key: Theme paragraph rubric: 4 = clear claim, two exact quotations with page numbers, each explained, concluding sentence; 3 = claim and evidence with partial explanation; 2 = summary with weak claim; 1 = no claim/evidence. Fluency: expressive reading with appropriate phrasing and pace.

weeks.prep: Preview chapters 18–19 and the epilogue of Hatchet. Prepare an essay organizer (thesis, 3 reasons, quotations). Write the Unit 2 test.
misconceptions: A thesis that is a fact ('Brian is in Hatchet'). A thesis is an arguable claim.
Body paragraphs with quotes but no explanation. Use quote sandwich: introduce, quote, explain.
Forgetting transitions between paragraphs.

days.guide: Read chapters 18–19 and the epilogue. Discuss how the epilogue (facts about his rescue and life afterward) changes our view of his experience.

questions.q: How is Brian rescued?
questions.a: He retrieves the survival pack from the plane; it contains an emergency transmitter he switches on, and a pilot lands on the lake to rescue him.

questions.q: How long was Brian alone?
questions.a: 54 days.

days.guide: Your child chooses a prompt and fills the organizer: thesis, three reasons, quotations for each. Check that the thesis is arguable and that each reason has at least one quotation with a page number before drafting.

questions.q: Model thesis for 'How does Brian change?'
questions.a: Brian changes from a frightened, self-pitying city boy into a patient, observant survivor who solves problems himself.

days.guide: Draft the five-paragraph essay; introduction with thesis, three body paragraphs, conclusion. Write one body paragraph together as a model if needed; your child drafts the rest. Expect this to take the full lesson.

questions.q: What goes in a conclusion?
questions.a: A restated thesis in new words and a final thought about why the change matters.

days.guide: Revise for transitions and explanation; edit for perfect tenses and spelling. Read the essay aloud together; your child adds a transition at the start of each body paragraph and one more sentence of explanation after each quotation.

questions.q: Name 3 transitions for body paragraphs.
questions.a: First, In addition, Finally (also: For example, However, As a result).

days.guide: Give the Unit 2 test and collect the final essay. Give the test without help, then score the essay separately with the rubric and return both with one specific compliment and one goal.

questions.q: Does Brian tell his father about the Secret?
questions.a: The epilogue says he never told his father.

weeks.assessment_key: Essay rubric (4 levels): 4 = arguable thesis, three well-developed body paragraphs each with a quotation and explanation, transitions, conclusion, few errors; 3 = all parts present with some thin explanation; 2 = weak thesis or missing evidence; 1 = incomplete. Unit 2 test key (suggested): 1) Brian is going to visit his father 2) the hatchet was from his mother 3) fire from sparks on rock 4) the low point follows the plane passing overhead 5) the moose and tornado destroy his shelter 6) the tornado lifts the plane's tail into view 7) a transmitter brings rescue after 54 days 8) theme: resilience/learning from mistakes 9) simile vs metaphor labeled 10) spect/port/struct/rupt meanings.

weeks.prep: Print ReadWorks articles on exploration and navigation, text-structure graphic organizers and a dictionary. Write 10 short paragraphs (or use the articles) for sorting.
misconceptions: Mixing up cause/effect and problem/solution. Problem/solution names a problem and how people fixed it; cause/effect explains why something happened.
Picking structure by one signal word only. Read the whole paragraph's purpose.
A summary with opinions or tiny details. Summaries are objective and focus on main ideas.

days.guide: Teach five structures and signal words: description (for example), sequence/chronology (first, then, in 1492), compare/contrast (however, both), cause/effect (because, as a result), problem/solution (the problem was, solved). Your child sorts 10 paragraphs.

questions.q: Signal words 'first, next, in 1519' suggest which structure?
questions.a: Chronological (sequence).

questions.q: 'Sailors couldn't find longitude, so the chronometer was invented' — structure?
questions.a: Problem/solution.

days.guide: Read two navigation articles and chart their structures and what each structure helps the reader understand. Ask: 'Why did each author choose that structure?' The child should connect structure to purpose.

questions.q: Why might an author use chronology for navigation tools?
questions.a: To show how tools developed over time, from early methods to modern ones.

days.guide: Your child defines 10 navigation terms with context and dictionary and draws two. Your child writes the context clue, the dictionary definition, and a sentence of their own for each word.

questions.q: What is latitude?
questions.a: Distance north or south of the equator, measured in degrees.

questions.q: What is a compass used for?
questions.a: Finding direction; its magnetic needle points north.

days.guide: Identify two main ideas in an Age of Exploration article; your child writes a 5-sentence summary. Model finding the main idea of one paragraph by asking what most sentences are about. Check that the summary has no opinions.

questions.q: Name a main reason for the Age of Exploration.
questions.a: Europeans wanted new sea routes to Asia for spices and trade (also wealth, power and spreading religion).

days.guide: Give the text-structure quiz and vocabulary check. Score both, then review any structure your child confused using the signal-word chart.

questions.q: What does a sextant measure?
questions.a: The angle between the horizon and the sun or a star, used to find latitude.

weeks.assessment_key: Text structure quiz: student correctly names description, sequence, compare/contrast, cause/effect and problem/solution for given paragraphs (8/10 = proficient). Vocabulary check key: compass (direction), sextant (angle of sun/star above horizon), latitude (N–S of equator), longitude (E–W of prime meridian), navigator, chart (sea map). Summary: objective, 5 sentences, two main ideas.

weeks.prep: Find an excerpt of Columbus's journal from October 1492 (Library of Congress or National Archives education sites) and the Smithsonian NMAI article on the Taíno. Preview both — the journal describes the Taíno as potential servants, which should be discussed honestly.
misconceptions: Believing primary sources are always objective. A primary source shows the author's view and goals.
Thinking the Taíno disappeared entirely. Their population was devastated by disease, violence and forced labor, but Taíno descendants and culture continue today in the Caribbean and elsewhere.
Mixing up Greek roots graph (write) and gram (letter/written).

days.guide: Read the journal excerpt; your child notes how Columbus describes the land and the Taíno and what he seems to want. Read it together slowly, defining old words; your child highlights descriptions of people in one color and of land in another.

questions.q: How does Columbus describe the Taíno?
questions.a: As gentle, friendly, well-built people who had no iron weapons; he writes that they would make good servants and could easily be converted to Christianity.

questions.q: What does that show about his goals?
questions.a: He was looking for gold, lands and people to control for Spain.

days.guide: Read the secondary source about Taíno life (farming, villages, canoes, cassava) and the effects of contact; note the author's point of view. Ask what the author wants readers to understand and which words reveal that view.

questions.q: What happened to the Taíno after contact?
questions.a: Many died from European diseases, violence and forced labor under Spanish rule.

days.guide: Chart what each account emphasizes and leaves out, quoting both. Your child needs at least one exact quotation from each source. Ask, 'Whose voice is missing from the journal?'

questions.q: What does Columbus's journal leave out?
questions.a: The Taíno point of view and the harm that followed.

days.guide: Discuss why accounts differ (purpose, audience, experience). Teach graph (write), tele (far), geo (earth), chron (time).

questions.q: What does 'chronology' mean? 'telegraph'?
questions.a: The order of events in time; a device that 'writes from far away' (sends messages over distance).

days.guide: Your child writes a point-of-view paragraph with quotations and takes a Greek roots quiz. Review the paragraph against the rubric, then grade the roots quiz.

questions.q: What does 'geography' mean by its roots?
questions.a: geo (earth) + graph (write) = writing about/describing the earth.

weeks.assessment_key: Paragraph rubric: 4 = explains both points of view, two accurate quotations, explains why they differ (purpose/perspective); 3 = both views with one quotation; 2 = summary only; 1 = inaccurate. Greek roots quiz key: graph = write; tele = far; geo = earth; chron = time; e.g., autograph, telescope, geology, chronological.

weeks.prep: Borrow 'And Then What Happened, Paul Revere?' by Jean Fritz; preview it. Gather note cards and visit the library catalog.
misconceptions: Treating a biography as a story with made-up parts. Biographies are factual, though authors choose which details to emphasize.
Writing research questions answerable with yes/no. Use how/why/what questions.
Underlining article titles. Underline or italicize book titles; put article and chapter titles in quotation marks.

days.guide: Read the biography; your child builds a timeline of Revere's life events (born in Boston, silversmith, Sons of Liberty, Boston Tea Party, midnight ride in April 1775). Read aloud together; Fritz's humor makes it quick. Your child adds a date or age to each timeline event where the book gives one.

questions.q: What was Paul Revere's trade?
questions.a: Silversmith (he also made engravings and other metalwork).

questions.q: Why is the book called 'And Then What Happened'?
questions.a: Revere was always busy with one activity after another, and Fritz keeps the story moving through his many adventures and mishaps.

days.guide: Your child completes a cause/effect chart on how the Sons of Liberty, the British, and his trade influenced Revere. Model one cause/effect row, then have your child explain each row aloud.

questions.q: How did the British influence Revere's actions?
questions.a: British taxes and soldiers in Boston made him join the Patriots, take part in the Boston Tea Party and ride to warn of troop movements.

days.guide: Your child chooses a colonial life or explorer topic and writes 4 research questions on different aspects. Check that each question asks how or why and that the four questions cover different aspects (food, work, school, homes).

questions.q: Rewrite as an open question: Did colonists make candles?
questions.a: How did colonists make candles, and why were they important?

days.guide: Find 3 sources and record a source list with titles correctly formatted. Show how to judge a website (who wrote it, .gov/.edu/.org, date). Your child records author, title and publisher for each.

questions.q: Format: book Colonial Times; article Daily Life.
questions.a: Colonial Times (italicized or underlined); “Daily Life” in quotation marks.

days.guide: Give a quiz on the biography and title punctuation; conference on the research questions. During the conference, help your child cut or sharpen any question that is too broad.

questions.q: What happened to Revere at the end of the midnight ride?
questions.a: British soldiers stopped and captured him; they took his horse and he did not reach Concord.

weeks.assessment_key: Cause/effect chart: three accurate causes with effects. Research questions: 4 open-ended questions on different aspects. Title punctuation quiz key: books, magazines, films italicized/underlined; stories, poems, articles, songs in quotation marks. Biography quiz (suggested): silversmith; Boston; Sons of Liberty; Boston Tea Party; ride to warn that the British were coming; captured before Concord.

weeks.prep: Have note cards, the week 12 sources and an outline template ready. Model one paraphrased card yourself.
misconceptions: Paraphrasing by swapping a few words. Read, cover the text, write from memory, then check.
Forgetting to label sources on note cards. Code each card with question # and source letter.
Introduction that just says 'My report is about…'. Use a hook and preview the subtopics.

days.guide: Model one card: source code, question number, paraphrase in your own words. Your child makes 15 cards from 3 sources.

questions.q: What goes on every note card?
questions.a: The source, the research question it answers, and a fact in your own words (quotation marks if copied exactly).

days.guide: Your child paraphrases 5 passages and compares to the originals, then finishes cards. Show a copied sentence with a few words swapped and explain why it is still plagiarism. Then use 'read, cover, write, check.'

questions.q: What is plagiarism?
questions.a: Using someone else's words or ideas as your own without credit.

days.guide: Sort cards into 3–4 subtopics and build an outline with headings. Lay the cards on the table and let your child physically group them; name each group as a heading.

questions.q: How do you choose headings?
questions.a: Group cards that answer the same question; name each group with a short topic heading.

days.guide: Draft introduction and two body sections with transitions. Your child writes from the outline, one section per heading, starting each section with a topic sentence.

questions.q: Use 'however' correctly in a sentence.
questions.a: Colonial children worked hard; however, they also played games like marbles.

days.guide: Finish the draft with a conclusion and source list; self-check against the informative rubric. Have your child read the rubric aloud and mark where the draft meets each line.

questions.q: What does a conclusion do in an informative report?
questions.a: Restates the main ideas and leaves the reader with a final thought.

weeks.assessment_key: Note cards: 15 cards, each coded, paraphrased, accurate. Outline: 3–4 headed subtopics with supporting facts. Informative draft rubric: 4 = clear intro with hook and focus, organized sections with facts, transitions, conclusion, source list; 3 = all parts, some thin sections; 2 = disorganized or copied text; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Computer, poster board or slideshow program, presentation checklist. Pick two short informational articles on the same topic for the cold read.
misconceptions: Adding text features that don't connect to the text. Each feature needs a caption explaining it.
Reading slides word for word. Slides show key points; the speaker explains.
Comparing two texts by summarizing each separately. Integrate: say how they agree, differ and add to each other.

days.guide: Your child revises for precise vocabulary, adds one quotation and one text feature (map, diagram or timeline). Help your child choose a feature that adds information the words cannot show easily, and write a caption for it.

questions.q: Replace with a domain word: The colonists used the big pot to make soap.
questions.a: The colonists used the kettle to make lye soap (any precise term).

days.guide: Type the final report and edit for commas, title punctuation and spelling. Typing in one sitting builds stamina; afterward your child edits a printed copy with a pen.

questions.q: Punctuate the title: I read the article colonial kitchens.
questions.a: I read the article “Colonial Kitchens.”

days.guide: Create a poster or 4 slides with captioned images highlighting the main ideas. Each slide or poster section gets a heading, a few key words and a captioned image — not paragraphs.

questions.q: What should a caption do?
questions.a: Explain what the image shows and how it connects to the report.

days.guide: Your child presents for 3–4 minutes and answers two questions. Rehearse once first. During the talk, note eye contact, volume and pace on the checklist.

questions.q: Give two speaking tips.
questions.a: Make eye contact, speak loudly and clearly at a steady pace.

days.guide: Give the cold-read comparison of two informational texts (structure, point of view, integration). Choose two short articles on one topic. Do not help during the assessment; score it afterward with the rubric.

questions.q: How do you integrate two texts?
questions.a: State what both say, what each adds that the other doesn't, and how together they explain the topic better.

weeks.assessment_key: Report rubric (4 levels): 4 = focused, well-organized, accurate facts with precise vocabulary, quotation, text feature, sources listed, few errors; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = missing parts or many errors; 1 = incomplete. Presentation checklist: 3–4 minutes, clear voice, eye contact, visual used, answered 2 questions. Unit 3 cold-read: proficient answers name each text's structure, describe each author's point of view, and combine information from both with evidence.

weeks.prep: Print 'Paul Revere's Ride' by Longfellow (Poetry Foundation). Keep the Jean Fritz biography handy for comparison.
misconceptions: Believing the poem is accurate history. Longfellow (1860) changed facts to create a national hero.
Confusing stanza and line. A stanza is a group of lines.
Labeling rhyme scheme by counting lines instead of end sounds.

days.guide: Read aloud with drama. Your child writes a one-line summary for each stanza.

questions.q: What does 'One if by land, and two if by sea' mean?
questions.a: One lantern in the Old North Church tower if the British come by land, two if they cross the river by boat.

days.guide: Mark the rhyme scheme and galloping rhythm in the first three stanzas; explain how sound matches action. Clap the beat of a few lines together. Label end sounds with letters (A, B) to find the pattern.

questions.q: Rhyme scheme of stanza 1 (hear / Revere / Seventy-five / alive / year)?
questions.a: AABBA.

questions.q: How does the rhythm match the action?
questions.a: The quick da-da-DUM beat sounds like galloping hooves.

days.guide: Compare the poem with Fritz's biography; list changes Longfellow made. Make a two-column chart: 'In the poem' vs. 'What really happened.' Ask why a poet might change facts.

questions.q: What did Longfellow change?
questions.a: Revere actually arranged the lantern signal for others; other riders (William Dawes, Samuel Prescott) also rode; Revere was captured and never reached Concord.

questions.q: Why might he change it?
questions.a: To create a simple, inspiring hero story for Americans before the Civil War.

days.guide: Your child illustrates the three most vivid images and labels the words that created each. Your child copies the exact words under each drawing and circles the sensory words.

questions.q: Name a vivid image from the poem.
questions.a: The lantern shining in the belfry of the Old North Church; the horse's hoof sparks in the dark.

days.guide: Recite two memorized stanzas; give the poetry terms quiz. Have your child practice the stanzas daily this week; give the quiz after the recitation.

questions.q: Define imagery.
questions.a: Words that create pictures in the reader's mind using the senses.

weeks.assessment_key: Recitation: memorized accurately, expressive. Poetry terms quiz key: stanza = group of lines; rhyme scheme = pattern of end rhymes (AABBA in stanza 1); rhythm = beat pattern; imagery = sensory pictures; narrative poem = tells a story. Poem vs. history chart: at least 3 accurate differences.

weeks.prep: Print 'The Road Not Taken' and 'Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening' by Robert Frost and 'Hope is the thing with feathers' by Emily Dickinson. Make a list of 12 idioms/proverbs.
misconceptions: Reading 'The Road Not Taken' as simply 'always choose the unusual path.' The speaker admits the roads were 'really about the same'; it is about choices and how we tell our story later.
Taking idioms literally. Explain figurative meanings.
Thinking the repeated last line in 'Stopping by Woods' is a mistake. Repetition adds weight.

days.guide: Read twice; discuss what the roads symbolize; your child writes the theme in one sentence. Read it twice aloud. Ask: Were the roads really different? (The poem says they were 'really about the same.') What does the speaker say he will tell 'ages and ages hence'?

questions.q: What do the two roads represent?
questions.a: Choices in life.

questions.q: Write a theme.
questions.a: The choices we make shape our lives, even when we can't know where they will lead.

days.guide: Analyze the speaker's point of view and the repeated last line; mark rhyme scheme. Ask who is speaking, where he is, and what pulls him to stay and what makes him leave. Label end rhymes A, B.

questions.q: Why does Frost repeat 'And miles to go before I sleep'?
questions.a: It emphasizes the speaker's duties and long journey; the second time it can also suggest life and death.

questions.q: Rhyme scheme of stanza 1?
questions.a: AABA.

days.guide: Chart how hope is compared to a bird in each stanza. Make a three-row chart, one per stanza: what the bird does and what that says about hope.

questions.q: What does it mean that hope 'never stops - at all'?
questions.a: Hope keeps singing inside us even in hard times.

questions.q: What does the bird ask in return?
questions.a: Nothing — 'never… asked a crumb' of the speaker.

days.guide: Teach 12 idioms/proverbs; your child connects two to the poems. Teach the idioms with literal-vs-real-meaning sketches. Ask which idiom fits the choice in 'The Road Not Taken.'

questions.q: Meaning of 'cross that bridge when you come to it'?
questions.a: Don't worry about a problem until it happens.

days.guide: Your child writes an extended-metaphor poem (e.g., 'Courage is…') and takes an idioms quiz. Brainstorm what the abstract idea would look, sound and act like before drafting. Grade the quiz afterward.

questions.q: What is an extended metaphor?
questions.a: A comparison continued through several lines or the whole poem.

weeks.assessment_key: Metaphor poem rubric: 4 = one metaphor sustained across the poem with vivid details; 3 = metaphor sustained most of the poem; 2 = several unrelated comparisons; 1 = no metaphor. Idioms quiz key (sample): 'break the ice' = start a conversation; 'piece of cake' = easy; 'the early bird catches the worm' = acting early brings success; 'don't count your chickens before they hatch' = don't assume success too early. Theme sentences: complete statements about life.

weeks.prep: Print 'Dreams' and 'April Rain Song' by Langston Hughes and 'Jabberwocky' by Lewis Carroll. Gather art supplies for the anthology. Choose an unfamiliar poem for the cold read.
misconceptions: Thinking nonsense words have no meaning. Grammar position shows part of speech.
Free verse = no rules. It has no regular rhyme/meter but still uses line breaks and imagery deliberately.
Thinking informal language is wrong. Choose register to fit audience and purpose.

days.guide: Read the Hughes poems; identify metaphor (life is a broken-winged bird) and personification (let the rain kiss you). Your child writes a free-verse weather poem.

questions.q: What metaphors does Hughes use in 'Dreams'?
questions.a: If dreams die, life is a broken-winged bird that cannot fly; if dreams go, life is a barren field frozen with snow.

questions.q: Example of personification in 'April Rain Song'?
questions.a: 'Let the rain kiss you' or 'the rain sing you a lullaby.'

days.guide: Read 'Jabberwocky'; use grammar to decide the part of speech of 8 nonsense words. Model the first line: a word after 'the' is a noun; a word after 'did' is a verb. Your child completes a chart of 8 words with part of speech and an invented meaning.

questions.q: In 'the slithy toves did gyre and gimble,' what parts of speech are slithy, toves, gyre?
questions.a: slithy = adjective, toves = noun, gyre = verb.

days.guide: Compare formal and informal registers; your child rewrites a stanza in a different register. Discuss when informal language fits (friends) and when formal fits (speeches). Your child rewrites one stanza and explains the change.

questions.q: Rewrite formally: Hold on to your dreams, ok?
questions.a: Hold fast to your dreams.

days.guide: Compile 5 original poems into an illustrated anthology. Your child revises and copies each poem neatly, adds an illustration and a table of contents.

questions.q: Name the 5 required poem types.
questions.a: Narrative stanza, metaphor, free verse, rhyming, nonsense.

days.guide: Hold a poetry café reading of 2 original poems; give the cold-read poetry assessment. Set up snacks and an audience; then give the cold read independently and score it with the rubric.

questions.q: What is the theme of 'Dreams'?
questions.a: Hold on to your dreams because life without them is empty and limited.

weeks.assessment_key: Anthology rubric: 4 = all 5 types present, each uses its feature well, illustrated, polished; 3 = all present, minor issues; 2 = missing types; 1 = incomplete. Performance: clear, expressive. Cold-read: theme stated as full sentence; two figurative language examples identified and explained.

weeks.prep: Borrow Esperanza Rising by Pam Muñoz Ryan; preview the first four chapters. Parental note: Papa is killed by bandits and the family's house is burned. Find maps of Mexico and California.
misconceptions: Thinking third-person limited means the narrator knows everyone's thoughts. It follows mainly Esperanza's thoughts and feelings.
Skipping Spanish words. Use context; many are explained in the next sentence.
Listing traits without evidence. Each trait needs an example from the text.

days.guide: Read 'Las Uvas'; your child lists 5 details about El Rancho de las Rosas and locates Aguascalientes. Read aloud together; your child jots setting details as you go. Find Aguascalientes in central Mexico on the map.

questions.q: Describe Esperanza's life at the start.
questions.a: She lives a wealthy, privileged life on a large ranch with servants, beautiful clothes and a loving father.

questions.q: What tradition does Papa share at the harvest?
questions.a: Esperanza cuts the first bunch of grapes, and Papa teaches her to listen to the heartbeat of the land.

days.guide: Read 'Las Papayas'; discuss how Papa's death changes everything; define Spanish words in context. Your child makes a list of Spanish words with the context clue and a guessed meaning, checking later in a dictionary.

questions.q: How does Papa's death change things?
questions.a: Papa's stepbrothers, Tío Luis and Tío Marco, take control of the ranch's future; Tío Luis wants to marry Mama, and when she refuses, the house is burned.

days.guide: Your child explains third-person limited point of view with 2 quotations. Explain: the narrator says 'she' but shows only Esperanza's thoughts. Your child finds 2 quotations showing her feelings.

questions.q: Why tell the story from Esperanza's view?
questions.a: Readers experience her loss and see her pride and later her growth as she learns.

days.guide: Read 'Los Higos' and 'Las Guayabas'; build a character trait web with evidence. Your child adds at least 4 traits, each with a quotation and page number. Discuss which traits might change.

questions.q: How do they escape?
questions.a: Hidden in a wagon under guavas with Alfonso, Hortensia and Miguel; Abuelita stays behind to recover.

questions.q: One trait of Esperanza?
questions.a: Proud or spoiled — she thinks she is above the servants.

days.guide: Give a chapter quiz; your child writes a journal entry as Esperanza leaving Mexico. Grade the quiz; the journal entry should mention real details (the wagon, Abuelita, the blanket).

questions.q: What does Abuelita give Esperanza before she leaves?
questions.a: The blanket she has been crocheting, to finish.

weeks.assessment_key: Chapter quiz (suggested): 1) Papa was killed by bandits 2) Tío Luis wanted to marry Mama 3) the house was burned 4) they escape hidden in a wagon under guavas 5) Abuelita stays behind 6) the family goes to California. Trait web: 4 traits with evidence. Journal: first-person, accurate feelings and events.

weeks.prep: Preview chapters 'Los Melones' through 'Las Almendras' in Esperanza Rising. Venn diagram ready.
misconceptions: Thinking correlative conjunctions can be mixed (either/nor). They come in fixed pairs.
Seeing Esperanza's attitude change as sudden. It is gradual and has setbacks.
Subject-verb agreement with neither/nor: the verb agrees with the closer subject.

days.guide: Read 'Los Melones' (the train). Discuss Esperanza's treatment of the peasant girl and her attitude toward riding with poor people.

questions.q: How does Esperanza treat the peasant girl who wants to touch her doll?
questions.a: She pulls the doll away; Mama is ashamed and makes her see that she was unkind.

days.guide: Read 'Las Cebollas'; compare old and new homes in a Venn diagram. Your child fills each side of the Venn diagram with at least 3 details and finds 2 things that stayed the same.

questions.q: How is her new home different?
questions.a: A small cabin in a farm labor camp with shared bathrooms, instead of a large ranch house with servants.

days.guide: Teach either/or, neither/nor, both/and, not only/but also; your child writes 8 sentences about the novel. Write the four pairs on cards; your child matches them, then writes 8 sentences about the novel using each pair twice.

questions.q: Complete: Esperanza knew neither how to sweep ___ how to change a diaper.
questions.a: nor

days.guide: Read 'Las Almendras'; your child writes a paragraph on what Esperanza learns from sweeping the platform. Discuss how it felt to be laughed at; then your child writes a paragraph with a claim and two pieces of evidence.

questions.q: What does Esperanza learn?
questions.a: She learns that she lacks practical skills and that she must work and learn to survive; embarrassment teaches her humility.

days.guide: Book talk on how Esperanza is changing; quiz on chapters and correlative conjunctions. In the book talk, your child names one way Esperanza has changed and one way she has not yet changed.

questions.q: Who is Isabel?
questions.a: Hortensia and Alfonso's niece — Juan and Josefina's young daughter who admires Esperanza.

weeks.assessment_key: Venn: 3+ details each side and shared. Paragraph: claim about what she learns, 2 pieces of evidence. Grammar quiz key: either/or, neither/nor, both/and, not only/but also used correctly in 8 sentences.

weeks.prep: Preview 'Las Ciruelas,' 'Las Papas' and 'Los Aguacates.' Find a ReadWorks/CommonLit article on 1930s farmworkers and Mexican repatriation and read it first.
misconceptions: Confusing homographs with homophones. Homographs are spelled the same (wind/wind); homophones sound the same (to/too).
Thinking one side of the strike is simply right. Show both have reasons.
Ignoring historical context. The Great Depression shaped events.

days.guide: Read 'Las Ciruelas'; your child lists Marta's and Miguel's arguments about striking. Your child makes a two-column chart and adds a page number for each argument.

questions.q: What does Marta want?
questions.a: Workers should strike for better pay and living conditions.

questions.q: What does Miguel think?
questions.a: He wants to keep working and support his family; striking could cost them their jobs.

days.guide: Read 'Las Papas'; explain how Mama's illness changes Esperanza's responsibilities. Ask your child to list three new jobs or worries Esperanza takes on and the evidence for each.

questions.q: What illness does Mama get?
questions.a: Valley Fever, after a dust storm.

questions.q: How does Esperanza respond?
questions.a: She takes a job to earn money and care for the family.

days.guide: Read the article; note 3 facts the novel reflects. Read the article together first. Your child writes each fact and the matching event from the novel side by side.

questions.q: What was Mexican repatriation?
questions.a: During the Great Depression, many Mexicans and Mexican Americans (including U.S. citizens) were pressured or forced to leave the U.S.

days.guide: Read 'Los Aguacates'; practice synonyms, antonyms, homographs. Model homographs by saying both pronunciations. Your child sorts 15 words into synonyms, antonyms and homograph pairs.

questions.q: Two meanings of 'lead'?
questions.a: To guide (rhymes with seed); a metal (rhymes with bed).

days.guide: Your child writes a 'Two Sides' paragraph and takes a word relationships quiz. The paragraph must explain both sides fairly before giving an opinion; then grade the quiz.

questions.q: Antonym of 'generous'?
questions.a: Selfish.

weeks.assessment_key: Two-sides paragraph: 4 = both positions explained with evidence and a reasoned opinion; 3 = both sides, little evidence; 2 = one side; 1 = off topic. Word quiz: synonyms, antonyms and homographs correctly identified (e.g., wind = moving air / to turn; bow = bend / ribbon).

weeks.prep: Preview 'Los Espárragos,' 'Los Duraznos' and 'Las Uvas.' Prepare a theme organizer.
misconceptions: Thinking the novel ends where it began with no change. The grapes return but Esperanza is changed.
Thinking a symbol is just an object. A symbol stands for an idea.
Believing Miguel betrayed her. He used the money orders to bring Abuelita.

days.guide: Read 'Los Espárragos'; discuss the discovery that the money orders are gone and Esperanza's feeling of betrayal. Read together and stop at the discovery. Ask your child to predict what happened to the money orders and why.

questions.q: Why does Esperanza think Miguel betrayed her?
questions.a: Her saved money orders for bringing Abuelita are missing and Miguel has left.

days.guide: Read 'Los Duraznos'; track the phoenix and blanket symbols. Your child finds every mention of the phoenix and the blanket they can and explains what each moment shows.

questions.q: What does the phoenix symbolize?
questions.a: Rising from the ashes — starting over and being reborn after disaster.

questions.q: What does the blanket symbolize?
questions.a: Life's ups and downs (zigzag mountains and valleys) and Abuelita's love.

days.guide: Read 'Las Uvas'; explain why the novel ends with grapes. Compare the first and last chapters side by side: what is the same, and what is different about Esperanza?

questions.q: Why end with grapes?
questions.a: It shows a full circle: Esperanza is now on her birthday again but changed — humble and hopeful, with Abuelita back.

days.guide: Your child writes 2 theme statements with 3 pieces of evidence each. Model one theme as a complete sentence. Evidence should come from the beginning, middle and end of the novel.

questions.q: Theme example.
questions.a: Do not be afraid to start over; or, true wealth is family and love, not possessions.

days.guide: Give the whole-novel reading assessment. Give it without help; afterward review missed questions by returning to the text.

questions.q: How does Esperanza change?
questions.a: From a spoiled, proud girl to a hardworking, compassionate young woman who helps support her family.

weeks.assessment_key: Theme organizer: 2 statements, 3 pieces of evidence each from different parts of the novel. Novel assessment (suggested): 1) Papa's death 2) escape to California 3) Mama's Valley Fever 4) strike conflict 5) money orders and Miguel bringing Abuelita 6) phoenix = rebirth 7) blanket = ups and downs 8) Esperanza's change.

weeks.prep: Have both novels and a compare-contrast organizer. Choose two short stories with similar themes for the cold read.
misconceptions: Writing two separate summaries instead of comparing. Each paragraph should mention both books.
Overusing 'also.' Use contrast transitions: however, on the other hand, while.
Thinking dialect is incorrect English. It reflects characters and culture.

days.guide: Fill the organizer on how Brian and Esperanza face loss and change, with 2 quotations each. Model one row of the organizer, then your child finds 2 quotations from each book with page numbers.

questions.q: How are Brian and Esperanza similar?
questions.a: Both lose their old lives suddenly and must learn new skills and attitudes to survive.

days.guide: Draft the essay with block or point-by-point structure and contrast transitions. Explain both structures with a quick sketch, then let your child choose. Check that each paragraph mentions both books.

questions.q: How do they differ?
questions.a: Brian faces physical survival alone in nature; Esperanza faces poverty and hard work with her family and community.

days.guide: Compare language: Spanish words in Esperanza Rising vs. Paulsen's plain, short sentences; add a paragraph.

questions.q: Why include Spanish words?
questions.a: They show Esperanza's culture and the setting.

days.guide: Revise with a checklist, edit and type the final essay. Use the rubric as a checklist; your child types the final copy after revisions.

questions.q: Name a contrast transition.
questions.a: However.

days.guide: Discuss the novels in a book talk; give the cold-read comparison assessment. In the book talk, ask which character changed more and why. Give the cold read independently.

questions.q: Shared theme of both novels?
questions.a: Adversity can make a person stronger and wiser.

weeks.assessment_key: Essay rubric: 4 = clear thesis, organized comparison with similarities and differences, 2+ quotations per book explained, transitions, language paragraph; 3 = all parts, some thin; 2 = summaries without comparison; 1 = incomplete. Cold-read rubric (choose an unfamiliar grade-5 story from CommonLit): 4 = states a precise theme/central idea, explains character with 2+ exact quotations correctly punctuated and explained; 3 = accurate answer with at least one relevant quotation and explanation; 2 = accurate but general answer, evidence paraphrased or loosely connected; 1 = inaccurate or no evidence.

weeks.prep: Choose paired opinion articles (CommonLit/ReadWorks) on zoos or homework and a short student speech/news clip. Argument map sheets.
misconceptions: Thinking an opinion is evidence. Evidence is facts, statistics, examples or expert quotes.
Confusing the claim with a reason.
Assuming more evidence is better than relevant evidence.

days.guide: Read the article aloud together. Model finding the claim (often in the first or last paragraph), then your child fills the organizer with each reason and the evidence under it.

questions.q: What is a claim?
questions.a: The writer's main position.

days.guide: Define each type with an example. Your child sorts 10 evidence cards, then ranks the three strongest and explains why facts and expert quotes beat opinions.

questions.q: Classify: '80% of students said…'
questions.a: Statistic.

questions.q: Classify: 'Zoos are boring.'
questions.a: Opinion.

days.guide: Read both zoo articles, one per sitting if needed. Your child lists each author's reasons side by side and marks which are backed by evidence.

questions.q: One pro and one con reason about zoos?
questions.a: Pro: zoos protect endangered species through breeding and research. Con: animals may suffer in small enclosures.

days.guide: Watch a short speech or news segment twice: first for the main claim, then for reasons. Your child writes a 3-sentence summary of the claim and two reasons.

questions.q: What makes a speaker's reason convincing?
questions.a: It is supported by relevant evidence.

days.guide: Give a new short opinion article and the quiz without help. Score it, then reread together any reason your child mismatched.

questions.q: Which is a reason: 'Recess helps kids focus' or 'Recess should be longer'?
questions.a: 'Recess helps kids focus' is a reason; the other is the claim.

weeks.assessment_key: Argument maps: claim, 3 reasons, evidence matched. Quiz: proficient = correctly identifies claim and matches 4 of 5 reasons to evidence.

weeks.prep: Help your child gather 2+ sources on a debatable topic. Opinion organizer ready.
misconceptions: Choosing a question with no real sides.
Forgetting the comma after introductory elements.
Recording evidence without source names.

days.guide: Brainstorm 3–4 debatable questions together and pick one with real evidence on both sides. Your child writes an opinion statement that states a position and a preview of reasons.

questions.q: Is 'Recess is fun' a good opinion statement?
questions.a: No — make it debatable: 'Schools should have longer recess because it improves focus.'

days.guide: Help locate 2 reliable sources. Your child records 6 facts or quotes on cards, each with the source name, using quotation marks for exact words.

questions.q: Why record source names?
questions.a: To credit sources and show the evidence is reliable.

days.guide: Your child sorts the evidence cards into 3 piles and names each pile as a reason. Then order them, saving the most convincing for last.

questions.q: Why save the strongest reason for last?
questions.a: It leaves the reader with the most powerful point.

days.guide: Model three types: word (However,), phrase (After lunch,), clause (Because…,). Your child writes 10 sentences for the essay, each starting with an introductory element and comma.

questions.q: Punctuate: After lunch students need to move.
questions.a: After lunch, students need to move.

questions.q: Punctuate: Yes recess matters.
questions.a: Yes, recess matters.

days.guide: Conference: ask your child to explain the opinion and the strongest reason aloud. Then give the comma quiz.

questions.q: Punctuate: Because exercise helps the brain recess should be longer.
questions.a: Because exercise helps the brain, recess should be longer.

weeks.assessment_key: Organizer: debatable opinion, 3 reasons, 6 evidence items with sources. Comma quiz key: comma after introductory words (Yes, Well, However), phrases (After lunch,), and clauses (Because…, When…, If…).

weeks.prep: Have the opinion organizer and revision checklist ready.
misconceptions: Ignoring the other side. Addressing a counterclaim makes an argument stronger.
Ending abruptly. Conclusions restate and call to action.
Omitting commas in direct address ('Thanks Mom').

days.guide: Share 2–3 hook styles (question, surprising fact, short scene). Your child drafts an introduction with a hook, 1–2 sentences of background and the opinion statement.

questions.q: Write a hook for recess.
questions.a: Example: Imagine sitting still for six hours straight.

days.guide: Model one body paragraph: reason as topic sentence, evidence, then explanation using 'specifically' or 'consequently.' Your child drafts the other two.

questions.q: Use 'consequently.'
questions.a: Students sit for hours; consequently, they lose focus.

days.guide: Ask, 'What would someone who disagrees say?' Your child writes that counterclaim and answers it, then drafts a conclusion that restates the opinion and calls readers to act.

questions.q: Write a counterclaim sentence.
questions.a: Some people argue that longer recess takes away learning time; however, research shows breaks improve attention.

days.guide: Teach with examples: 'Yes, I agree.' 'It's late, isn't it?' 'Sam, come here.' Your child fixes dialogue examples, then revises the essay with the checklist.

questions.q: Punctuate: You agree don't you?
questions.a: You agree, don't you?

questions.q: Punctuate: Mom can I go?
questions.a: Mom, can I go?

days.guide: The listener gives two specific 'glows' (what works) and one 'grow' (what to fix). Your child revises the draft that day while the feedback is fresh.

questions.q: What is a 'grow'?
questions.a: A specific suggestion for improvement.

weeks.assessment_key: Draft rubric: introduction with hook and opinion; 3 body paragraphs each with reason + evidence; counterclaim addressed; conclusion with call to action. Comma items correct: Yes, …; …, isn't it?; Mom, ….

weeks.prep: Computer, debate note cards, timer. Arrange a family member or co-op partner to debate.
misconceptions: Attacking the person instead of the argument.
Reading the essay word for word as a speech.
Using slang in a formal debate.

days.guide: Your child types the essay in one sitting, adds a title and a source list at the end, and proofreads a printed copy.

questions.q: Where does the source list go?
questions.a: At the end.

days.guide: Show how to boil each paragraph into a key phrase on a card. Your child practices the 2-minute opening with a timer and writes a rebuttal for 2 counterarguments.

questions.q: What is a rebuttal?
questions.a: A response that answers the other side's argument.

days.guide: Set rules: opening statements, rebuttals, closings, each timed. Model formal phrases ('I respectfully disagree because…') and note your child's use of evidence.

questions.q: Formal: 'That's dumb.'
questions.a: I disagree with that point because…

days.guide: Your child writes the opponent's 2 best reasons fairly, then a paragraph on whether their own thinking changed and why.

questions.q: Why summarize the other side fairly?
questions.a: It shows understanding and helps you respond better.

days.guide: Give an unfamiliar opinion article with questions, then set a 30-minute timer for an on-demand opinion paragraph. Do not help; score both with the rubric.

questions.q: What does a strong on-demand paragraph include?
questions.a: A clear opinion, 2–3 reasons with evidence, and a concluding sentence.

weeks.assessment_key: Opinion essay rubric (4 levels): 4 = clear opinion, 3 well-supported reasons, counterclaim, logical transitions, strong conclusion, source list, few errors; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = weak support; 1 = incomplete. Debate observation: formal language, stayed in time, rebuttals relevant. Unit 6 on-demand: opinion + 2 reasons with evidence + conclusion = proficient.

weeks.prep: Get The Secret Garden by Frances Hodgson Burnett (Project Gutenberg). Preview chapters 1–7. Note: Mary's parents die of cholera in chapter 1.
misconceptions: Thinking Mary is simply mean. She is neglected and lonely.
Skipping dialect. Read it aloud slowly; it gets easier.
Thinking 'contrary' means sad. It means stubborn and disagreeable.

days.guide: Read chapters 1–2 (aloud or together). Your child lists 5 details that show Mary is contrary and then discusses why: think about how she was raised.

questions.q: Why is Mary so disagreeable?
questions.a: Her parents ignored her and servants gave her whatever she wanted, so she never learned kindness.

questions.q: What happens to her parents?
questions.a: They die in a cholera outbreak in India.

days.guide: Read chapters 3–4. Your child sketches the manor, the moor and the gardens, labeling details from the text (e.g., the moor's heather and endless wild land).

questions.q: Where is Misselthwaite Manor?
questions.a: On the edge of the moor in Yorkshire, England — a huge, gloomy house with about a hundred rooms, most shut up.

days.guide: Read Martha's lines aloud slowly. Your child rewrites 8 lines in standard English and discusses what dialect adds to the story.

questions.q: Translate 'Canna' tha' dress thysen?'
questions.a: Can't you dress yourself?

questions.q: Why include dialect?
questions.a: It makes characters realistic and shows Yorkshire's culture.

days.guide: Read chapters 5–7 together. Your child writes a prediction of what the key opens and who might be crying in the corridor, with clues from the text.

questions.q: What does the robin help Mary find?
questions.a: The buried key to the locked garden.

days.guide: Give the quiz, then have your child practice a Martha passage twice before reading it aloud for fluency.

questions.q: Why was the garden locked?
questions.a: Mr. Craven locked it after his wife died following an accident there ten years before.

weeks.assessment_key: Chapter quiz (suggested): 1) Mary is from India 2) parents died of cholera 3) she goes to live with her uncle, Mr. Craven 4) Martha is the cheerful Yorkshire maid 5) Ben Weatherstaff is the gardener 6) the robin shows Mary the key 7) the garden has been locked ten years. Setting drawing: house, moor, gardens labeled. Dialect translation: 6 of 8 accurate.

weeks.prep: Preview chapters 8–15 of The Secret Garden; prepare sentence-combining cards from the novel.
misconceptions: Thinking sentence combining just means adding 'and.' Use clauses, appositives and phrases.
Seeing Colin as just a villain. He is frightened and lonely like Mary was.
Confusing the garden being 'dead' with 'wick' (alive).

days.guide: Read chapters 8–10. Ask your child to make a two-column chart: the garden's condition and Mary's condition, finding parallels.

questions.q: How are Mary and the garden alike?
questions.a: Both seem neglected and dead but are actually alive inside and begin to grow with care.

days.guide: Read chapters 11–12. Your child writes a character sketch of Dickon with 3 traits, each backed by a quotation.

questions.q: Describe Dickon.
questions.a: Martha's brother, kind and cheerful, who can charm animals and knows how to make things grow.

days.guide: Model combining two short sentences with a clause or phrase, then expanding and reducing. Your child completes 12 cards and reads the improved versions aloud.

questions.q: Combine: Dickon played a pipe. Animals came to him.
questions.a: When Dickon played his pipe, animals came to him.

days.guide: Read chapters 13–15. Your child charts Mary and Colin: how each acts, why, and what they need.

questions.q: Who is Colin?
questions.a: Mr. Craven's sickly son, Mary's cousin, who believes he will die young.

days.guide: Brainstorm sights, sounds and smells of the spring garden from the book. Your child writes a paragraph using at least 3 combined sentences.

questions.q: What makes descriptive writing strong?
questions.a: Sensory details and precise words.

weeks.assessment_key: Character sketch: 3 traits each supported by a quotation. Descriptive paragraph: sensory details, combined sentences, varied beginnings. Comparison chart: similarities (spoiled, lonely, contrary) and differences (Colin bedridden, Mary active).

weeks.prep: Preview chapters 16–22. Optional: find an illustrated edition or the 1949/1993 film for visual comparison (preview first).
misconceptions: Thinking 'Magic' is literal. The children call the healing power of nature and positive thinking 'Magic.'
Thinking films must match books. Adaptations change things for the medium.
Missing Colin's turning point.

days.guide: Read chapters 16–18. Your child records Colin's attitude early (tantrums, fear of dying) and later, with quotations.

questions.q: What changes Colin?
questions.a: Mary's honesty, Dickon's stories, the idea of the garden and fresh air.

days.guide: Read chapters 19–20. Ask: What is Magic to the children? Your child explains with two quotations.

questions.q: What do they mean by Magic?
questions.a: The force that makes things grow and that heals Colin — nature and positive thinking.

days.guide: Show an illustration or a short film scene (previewed). Your child writes how colors, lighting or music create mood compared with the words.

questions.q: How can an illustration change mood?
questions.a: Colors, light and details can make a scene feel gloomy or joyful.

days.guide: Read chapters 21–22. Discuss why standing up matters so much to Colin and how it changes the story.

questions.q: Why does Colin stand?
questions.a: Ben Weatherstaff calls him a cripple with crooked legs, and Colin angrily stands to prove him wrong.

days.guide: Your child writes a theme paragraph about nature healing, with evidence from three different chapters, and checks it against the rubric.

questions.q: Theme?
questions.a: Nature, friendship and hope can heal both body and spirit.

weeks.assessment_key: Theme paragraph rubric: 4 = clear theme statement, evidence from three chapters, explained; 3 = two chapters; 2 = summary; 1 = none. Visual analysis: names one visual and explains its effect on mood.

weeks.prep: Preview chapters 23–27 and a script template. Plan family roles for readers' theater.
misconceptions: Writing a script as prose. Scripts use character names, dialogue and stage directions.
Forgetting the ending resolves Mr. Craven's story too.
Reading lines flatly.

days.guide: Read chapters 23–27; summarize how the ending resolves Mary's, Colin's and Mr. Craven's stories.

questions.q: How does the novel end?
questions.a: Mr. Craven returns home, finds Colin healthy in the garden, and walks with him across the lawn back to the house.

questions.q: How has Mary changed?
questions.a: She is healthy, kind and caring.

days.guide: Read a sample script together. Your child notes how scenes replace chapters, a cast list replaces descriptions, and stage directions show action.

questions.q: What are stage directions?
questions.a: Instructions in parentheses or italics telling actors how to move or speak.

days.guide: Your child picks a key chapter and writes 2 scenes: a cast list, dialogue from the book, and stage directions in parentheses.

questions.q: Format a line.
questions.a: MARY: (whispering) It's the key to the garden!

days.guide: Assign roles and read through twice. Coach on expression, pacing and Yorkshire dialect.

questions.q: How do you show emotion in readers' theater?
questions.a: With voice: tone, volume and pace.

days.guide: Perform the readers' theater for an audience. Then give the novel assessment independently and score it with the key.

questions.q: Who is Mrs. Medlock?
questions.a: The housekeeper at Misselthwaite.
